scenario: AITA for adopting a puppy when we were notified the foster wanted to adopt the puppy, we were notified after a week of adotion process | My fiancee, her son (9), and I just moved into a new house and finally have no restrictions on owning a dog. We have applied for several puppies through a local rescue/adoption agency. After sending 8 or 10 applications for various puppies and being put on waitlists we finally got the call that we were set for an interview. We had initially been second in line but something from the first interview didn't work out so we moved up to first in line the day after our application. We did an interview the next day and everything went well and the adoption coordinator said they would notify the foster home. The puppy had a final medical check for a small hip injury on the following Tuesday. On Monday we got an email from the foster family to start the process of setting up a meet and greet. Tuesday afternoon we got a call from the agency that the medical went well and the puppy is healthy. But they also told us that the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog. Typically the foster homes get first choice for adopting dogs they foster and the puppy should apparently never have been listed. The agency says they have bonded between the family and puppy. Because it was an error on the part of the agency and the puppy should never have been listed as available for adoptions, they have left the choice with us to either follow through and adopt the puppy or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We have been excited about this puppy since last Wednesday when we were first selected for an interview. Have already bought a collar and several toys for her and shown her to friends and family and told them we were in the process of adopting this beautiful puppy. Our nine year old son also loves the dog and is crushed by the news we may not get her now. Am I the asshole if we adopted the puppy and didn't let the foster family keep her?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm "the asshole" in this situation. Let me start by understanding what happened. We moved into a new house and finally have no restrictions on owning a dog. That's great! We applied for several puppies through a local rescue/adoption agency. We sent out 8 or 10 applications and got put on waitlists. Finally, we got a call that we were set for an interview. Initially, we were second in line, but something from the first interview didn't work out, so we moved up to first in line the day after our application. We did the interview the next day, and everything went well. The adoption coordinators said they would notify the foster home. The puppy had a final medical check for a small hip injury on the following Tuesday. On Monday, we got an email from the foster family to start the process of setting up a meet-and-greet. Tuesday afternoon, we got a call from the agency that the medical went well, and the puppy is healthy. But they also told us that the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog. Typically, foster homes get first choice for adopting dogs they foster, and the puppy should apparently never have been listed. The agency said they have bonded between the family and puppy. Because it was an error on the part of the agency and the puppy should never have been listed as available for adoptions, they have left the choice with us to either follow through and adopt the puppy or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We have been excited about this puppy since last Wednesday when we were first selected for an interview. We've already bought a collar and several toys for her and shown her to friends and family and told them we were in the process of adopting this beautiful puppy. Our nine-year-old son also loves the dog and is crushed by the news that we may not get her now. So, the question is: Am I the asshole if we adopt the puppy and didn't let the foster family keep her? First, I need to understand the dynamics here. Foster homes usually have the first choice to adopt the animals they care for. That makes sense because they've already invested time and emotional energy into the animal. It's a common practice in adoption agencies to give foster families priority. In this case, the agency made a mistake by listing the puppy as available for adoption when it shouldn't have been. That's their error. Now, they're giving us the choice to either proceed with the adoption or let the foster family keep the puppy. We've already invested emotionally and financially into this puppy. We've told our friends and family about her, bought supplies, and our son is really excited about her. It's understandable that we're upset and want to go through with the adoption. On the other hand, the foster family has likely formed a bond with the puppy as well. They were fostering her, and now they're interested in adopting her. It's their right, as per the agency's usual policy, to have first choice. So, the conflict arises because the agency made a mistake, and now we're caught in the middle. We have to decide whether to proceed with our adoption or let the foster family keep the puppy. If we decide to adopt the puppy despite the foster family's interest, are we being selfish? Are we disregarding the agency's usual policies and the foster family's emotional investment? Alternatively, if we let the foster family keep the puppy, we're letting go of something we've been excited about and have already invested in emotionally and financially. It's a tough spot. I think the key here is to consider the agency's mistake and the foster family's rights. Since the puppy shouldn't have been listed for adoption, the foster family should have the priority. However, we've already made plans and investments based on the information we had. Maybe the right approach is to communicate openly with the agency and the foster family. Express our feelings and see if there's a way to resolve this that's fair to everyone. Perhaps the agency can find another puppy for us, or the foster family can find another way to support us. In the end, it's a difficult situation, and there's no perfect solution. But being understanding and empathetic to both the foster family and the agency's mistake is important.
